title: Explain the Spring IoC container, the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext, Inversion of Control, and Dependency Injection vs Dependency Lookup.
shortTitle: What is IoC Container: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?
keyPoints: IoC is a design principle where the framework controls object creation and dependency wiring instead of your code doing it with the new keyword.
BeanFactory is the basic lazy-loading container interface that creates beans only when first requested.
ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory with eager initialization, event publishing, AOP integration, annotation scanning, and i18n support.
Dependency Injection means the container pushes dependencies into beans via constructors, setters, or fields.
Dependency Lookup means the bean pulls dependencies from the container using getBean() and is discouraged because it couples code to the Spring API.
Spring Boot creates an ApplicationContext automatically when you call SpringApplication.run().
The refresh() lifecycle loads bean definitions, invokes BeanFactoryPostProcessors, registers BeanPostProcessors, creates singletons, and publishes ContextRefreshedEvent.

s1_definition.oneliner: IoC means the container controls object creation and wiring instead of your code doing it with new; ApplicationContext is the full-featured container and BeanFactory is its minimal lazy-loading parent.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Inversion of Control (IoC)** -- a design principle where the framework manages object creation and dependency wiring instead of the application code doing it manually with the `new` keyword.
- **Dependency Injection (DI)** -- the mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC by pushing dependencies into beans via constructors, setters, or fields.
- **BeanFactory** -- the basic IoC container interface that uses lazy initialization, creating beans only when first requested.
- **ApplicationContext** -- the full-featured container that extends `BeanFactory` with eager initialization, event publishing, AOP proxy support, annotation scanning, `@Profile`, and i18n.
- **Dependency Lookup** -- a discouraged pattern where the bean pulls dependencies from the container via `applicationContext.getBean()`, coupling code to the Spring API.
s1_definition.analogy: Without IoC, every teller at National Bank of India builds their own desk, finds their own printer, and connects their own terminal. With IoC, the branch manager (Spring container) sets up everything before the teller arrives. The teller declares "I need a printer and a terminal" and the manager provides them. BeanFactory is a basic manager who fetches items only when asked (lazy). ApplicationContext is a senior manager who prepares everything before the bank opens (eager) and also handles announcements, security audits, and multilingual forms.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  ApplicationContext                   │
  │   (eager init, events, AOP, i18n, profiles)          │
  │                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │              BeanFactory                      │    │
  │  │   (lazy init, basic DI, singleton registry)   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  SpringApplication.run()
       │
       ▼
  refresh()
       │
       ├─── Load bean definitions (@ComponentScan, @Bean)
       ├─── BeanFactoryPostProcessors (resolve ${...})
       ├─── Register BeanPostProcessors
       ├─── Create ALL singletons (eager)
       │       ├── Instantiate (constructor)
       │       ├── Inject (@Autowired fields/setters)
       │       ├── BeanPostProcessor.before (@PostConstruct)
       │       └── BeanPostProcessor.after (AOP proxy)
       ├─── Publish ContextRefreshedEvent
       └─── Start embedded Tomcat
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Inversion of Control is a design principle where the framework takes responsibility for creating objects and wiring their dependencies, instead of the application code doing it with the new keyword. In Rajesh's banking transfer service at National Bank of India, the TransferService declares its dependency on AccountRepository as a final field in the constructor. Spring's IoC container scans for the JPA repository implementation, creates it, and injects it automatically. The TransferService never knows or cares whether it received a JPA repository, a JDBC repository, or a mock. This gives us testability: in unit tests, Rajesh creates the service with a mock repository using Mockito, with no Spring context and no database, making tests run in milliseconds.

Spring provides two IoC container implementations. BeanFactory is the basic interface with lazy bean initialization that creates beans only when first requested. ApplicationContext extends it with eager initialization that catches configuration errors at startup, automatic registration of BeanPostProcessors for annotation processing, event publishing, internationalization, and environment-aware profiles. Every Spring Boot application uses ApplicationContext because SpringApplication.run() creates one automatically. The eager initialization is particularly valuable in production because a missing dependency or invalid configuration fails the application at startup with a clear error, not at 3 AM when Priya's first loan application triggers the misconfigured code path.

The key architectural benefit of IoC is that it enforces the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules depend on abstractions, not implementations. When the National Bank of India migrated from JDBC to JPA, the team changed the repository implementation without modifying a single line of the TransferService or the TransferController. That is the real power of Inversion of Control.

Remember one sentence: IoC means the container creates and wires your objects so your code depends only on interfaces, never on implementations.
